claims.text: A network partition is a fault that splits a system into parts that keep running but cannot reach each other, so each part sees the others as unreachable.

The CAP theorem, a classic result in distributed systems: during a network partition a system holding copies of data cannot both answer every request (availability) and give only the latest value (consistency); it gives up one. P names partition tolerance.
claims.source_hint: The CAP conjecture and its formal proof (consistency = every read sees the latest write; availability = every request to a non-failing part gets an answer); outline item 2

claims.text: From the api's side a stopped database and one cut off by the network end the same way: every call fails, so both are treated as unreachable; a cut-off part cannot check that its copy still holds the latest value, because only the other side knows.

A networked system cannot rule partitions out (a broken cable, a misconfigured network between the machines), so the real choice is what each operation does while one lasts: answer with the copy it has, or refuse.
claims.source_hint: Outline item 3; same CAP proof as claim 2

claims.text: db-unreachable.sh reads product 3 first so Redis holds a copy, then stops the db container (line 37), and its trap on line 38 runs restore, which starts db again when the script ends.
Stopping the container differs from a real partition: a stopped server fails quickly, while in a real partition each call can wait until a timeout before it fails.
claims.source_hint: scripts/backend/db-unreachable.sh @ stage-4 lines 34-36; Npgsql connection string parameters (Timeout, Command Timeout); outline depth_notes

claims.text: With db stopped and a copy of product 3 in Redis, GET /api/v1/products/3 answers 200, GET /api/v1/products answers 500 and POST /api/v1/orders answers 500.

PlaceOrderAsync ends with SaveChangesAsync, saving the order in PostgreSQL, which owns orders. If a copy accepted it, the customer would hear 'received' while the owner has no record and reads from it miss the order; so while the owner is unreachable it can only refuse.
claims.source_hint: DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs @ stage-4 lines 17-52; docs/design/consistency-per-operation.md @ stage-4 line 16; outline item 5

claims.text: ProductCache's Redis copy expires 5 minutes after it was written (TTL set on write); on a miss it reads PostgreSQL, so once the copy expires during a partition product 3 fails too, and with no copy at all it fails like the list.
claims.source_hint: DonHang.Catalog/ProductCache.cs @ stage-4 lines 18, 25-49, 85-96; docs/design/consistency-per-operation.md line 13 ('không có bản sao thì lỗi')

claims.text: consistency-per-operation.md: one product answers from the Redis copy if present (old price OK); the list refuses though a slightly old list is OK, as no copy exists; placing an order refuses; the search row is not built at stage-4 and makes the list's choice.
Refund row: database unreachable -> refused, like an order; payment gateway unreachable -> still accepted, order stays refunding; no step reports a refund as done before the gateway confirms it.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/consistency-per-operation.md @ stage-4 line 18 and section 'Hoàn tiền'; DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs lines 82-95

claims.text: Viewing one's own order refuses during a partition because a customer who has just placed an order must see it at once; a copy can be older than that order.

Answer from a copy fits when an old value harms nobody; refuse fits when a lost or wrong answer costs more than no answer; save-and-finish-later fits when the slow part can wait and the in-between state is shown honestly.

If the business accepts a list a few minutes old, the product list may answer from a copy during a partition; change its row in consistency-per-operation.md first. Keep order views refusing unless the business drops its reason in writing.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/consistency-per-operation.md lines 14, 17 and final line ('Chuyển một thao tác khác ... cần sửa bảng trên trước')

claims.text: A transaction's consistency: the data still complies with the database's integrity constraints (e.g. a foreign key to an existing row) when it commits; CAP's consistency: every read sees the latest written value, wherever it is served from.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, Glossary 'Consistency'; CAP proof definition of consistency (claim 2); outline misconception 2

claims.text: The product page and placing an order both depend on the same db container, yet one answers during the partition and the other refuses, so the choice is per operation, not per database.
A design can make partitions rarer and shorter but cannot switch them off; during one, a cut-off part cannot both answer and guarantee the latest value.
POST /api/v1/orders/{id}/refund answers 202 once the order is refunding, before the gateway confirms.
